t: If an agent writes the draft, what should citizen developer training teach?
s: Autopilot is in preview as a coding agent in Studio Web. Starting from a 10-week citizen developer course we began at a large holding, how I would build it today.
b: Most citizen developer courses are judged by one question: after ten weeks, can the participant build an automation alone? I think that question has aged. UiPath’s Autopilot now runs as a coding agent in Studio Web, and it can take a requirement written in plain language, plan it and build a draft. If the agent writes the draft, three skills are left for the course to measure: reading what was generated, knowing which work is not yours to automate, and handing work over to the centre properly. What we delivered and what I recommend In February 2026 BOTTEQ started a 10-week UiPath Citizen RPA Developer course at a large holding. Our Automation & AI Solutions team lead taught it. The goal was to grow the number of citizen developers inside the organisation. I am not sharing the client’s name, the number of participants or the internal detail of the programme. The rest of this piece is not a record of that course. In February, Autopilot did not exist in Studio Web in its current form. The design below is what I would change if I built the same course today. The product facts come from UiPath’s own pages, listed at the end. What changed According to the Autopilot release notes, “Autopilot as a coding agent in Studio Web” was released in public preview on 23 September 2026; the note was added to the page two days later. UiPath describes it as the same coding agent that ships with Studio Desktop. Nothing needs installing. The user guide lists eight project types: Maestro Flow, Maestro BPMN, Maestro Case, agents, API workflows, RPA workflows, coded apps and functions. The use cases include planning an automation from a process definition document or a plain-language requirement and then building it, running a project and finding the cause of a failure, and explaining an unfamiliar project step by step. Support differs by project type, and that is the distinction that matters for a citizen developer. The Studio Web release notes say Autopilot builds API workflows from a description, then validates, runs and publishes them. For RPA workflows, coded apps and functions it currently reads, explains and reviews project files. So for the project type a business user builds most often, Autopilot in Studio Web is today mostly a reading and review assistant. Three things are written down on the administration side. t: Autopilot in production Orchestrator: seven steps for the approval mode
s: Autopilot Chat returned to Orchestrator on 28 October and can now manage queues, assets and triggers. A decision table for which approval mode belongs in which tenant, and seven checks before production.
b: The Autopilot Chat that came back to Orchestrator can manage processes, jobs, queues, assets, triggers, machines and folders in your tenant. That makes it an operator, and the decision that matters when you turn it on is which approval mode runs in which tenant. The documentation leaves two of the questions behind that decision open: what permissions Autopilot acts with, and what trail it leaves. The steps below are for closing those gaps before production. At BOTTEQ we work with clients on Orchestrator topology, tenant and environment design, asset and credential management and queue architecture. The product facts in this guide come from UiPath’s own pages, listed at the end. The recommendations and the decision table are my opinion. What changed UiPath removed Autopilot Chat from Orchestrator on 14 October, saying it would return with improved features. According to the 28 October release notes, it is back. The capability list in the user guide is broad: operating processes, jobs, queues, assets, triggers, machines, folders and storage buckets; investigating failed jobs and access issues; inspecting audit events; and planning, building and deploying automations. Projects themselves are created in Studio Web. You pick the approval mode from a dropdown under the chat box, and there are three: Cautious asks before every operation. UiPath calls it the safest option. Adaptive auto-approves known safe operations and is the one UiPath recommends. Turn on Smart approvals and it also approves operations the model judges safe. The page states plainly that the model can misjudge. Full access shows no approval prompts. The page says to use it only in trusted environments. Settings has five tabs: tools (such as web search and the web reader), built-in skills, MCP servers, personalisation (including a custom instruction added to every prompt), and a security tab that lists the sites Autopilot may use without asking and the ones it won’t open. The AI capabilities need an active AI Trust Layer policy deployed to the tenant. The feature availability table shows Autopilot Chat in Automation Cloud and Test Cloud, but not in the Public Sector or Dedicated offerings. Three things I could not find on the page: whether Autopilot acts with the signed-in user’s roles, who can connect an MCP server and whether that is scoped to a user or the tenant, and whether Autopilot’s own changes are logged separately. s: Issue five: more time for SMS approval of e-Müstahsil receipts, Türkiye’s electronic informed-consent rules, UiPath coded-agent governance, IXP and validation in Maestro Flow, Autopilot in Orchestrator, Gartner.
b: This week is about how approvals and records are kept. Türkiye’s revenue administration gave taxpayers eight more months to replace wet signatures on producer receipts with SMS verification, and the Ministry of Health set out the rules for taking patient consent the same way, with a one-time SMS code. On the platform side, UiPath is putting every agent under one governance policy from 2 December. GİB: deadline for SMS verification of e-Müstahsil receipts extended to 30 June 2027 Turkish Revenue Administration · 28 October 2026 On 22 May 2026 GİB had announced that the changes in its e-Müstahsil Makbuzu technical guide would be mandatory for every receipt issued from 5 November 2026. The e-Müstahsil Makbuzu is the electronic receipt issued when buying produce from a farmer, and the changes replace the farmer’s wet signature with verification through IT or communication channels. According to the 28 October announcement, GİB reviewed feedback from taxpayers and extended the deadline to 30 June 2027. Taxpayers who have finished the work can use the new method before then. Last week I wrote that I couldn’t find an effective date for this change in the e-Archive guide; it was in the May announcement, and it has now moved. Why it matters. A change that would have been mandatory this Thursday was pushed back at the last minute. That’s breathing room for teams who squeezed their project to hit 5 November, and a warning for those who haven’t started. My suggestion is to keep the scope and relax the schedule rather than let the work drift. Redesign the receipt flow around SMS approval and go live in a quiet period, outside harvest peaks, where the risk is lower. If you rely on an integrator, ask for a release plan against the new date. And if you already deployed a flow for 5 November that isn’t in use yet, don’t let it go stale. t: The EU softened its AI literacy rule, so build training around roles now
s: After the Digital Omnibus, Article 4 no longer sets a required level, but the duty remains and enforcement began in August 2026. How automation teams can build a small, role-based and recorded training plan.
b: The EU has softened the AI Act’s literacy article. According to the European Commission’s Q&A page, updated on 20 October, Article 4 as amended by the Digital Omnibus no longer requires a specific or “sufficient” level of AI literacy. The duty itself has not gone away: providers and deployers of AI systems must still take literacy measures for their staff. And the supervision and enforcement rules have applied since 2 August 2026. My reading is that the legal bar dropped while the business bar stayed where it was. If you treat the change as permission to trim the training budget, you have learned the wrong lesson. What changed and what didn’t The Commission’s page, in short: Question After the Omnibus Who is obliged? Providers and deployers of AI systems. The obligation remains. What level? No specific or “sufficient” level is mandated. Public sector role The Commission and Member States support the effort and publish practical examples. Enforcement Since 2 August 2026, by national market surveillance authorities rather than the AI Office. Certificate Not needed. Keeping an internal record of trainings is named as one way to show the work. High-risk systems Deployers must still make sure the staff doing human oversight are trained. Don’t skip the last row. The literacy article got looser, but if you deploy a high-risk system, training the people who oversee it is a separate obligation and it stands. The Commission also sketches a minimum: a general understanding of AI inside the organisation, clarity on whether you act as provider or deployer, and, depending on the risk of the systems in use, what staff need to know about those risks. A note from someone writing in Türkiye: these rules concern companies that place or use AI systems in the EU market. Check with your legal team whether you are in scope. Even if you aren’t, I think the plan below earns its keep on its own. The real reason isn’t in the regulation Gartner’s survey announcement of 19 October is headlined with the finding that only 13% of CIOs say their enterprise has realised significant or transformational value from AI. Gartner’s page refuses automated access, so I am relying on the headline alone. It says enough. I see most of the value leaking out on the human side. A business unit picks the wrong process. A validation clerk approves model output without questioning it. A manager can’t talk about cost or risk. None of that is fixed by a licence. As I have said publicly, in automation that is

t: AI Builder credits end on 1 November, and agents get tested in production
s: Issue four: the end of AI Builder credits, UiPath runtime evaluations for live agents and a new package feed, Agent Skills moving to the Linux Foundation, GİB changes to e-Müstahsil and UserList, and Gartner’s CIO survey.
b: This week is about infrastructure that changes quietly. The credit model behind document-processing flows in Power Automate changes on 1 November, UiPath is moving its package feed, and Türkiye’s revenue administration added mandatory fields to the e-Archive report schema. None of it makes headlines. Any of it can mean a robot that doesn’t start one morning. Microsoft: AI Builder capacity add-ons and seeded credits reach end of life on 1 November Microsoft Learn · Partner Center announcement 22 October 2026; calendar page 2 October 2026 Microsoft reminded partners that AI Builder capacity add-ons retire on 1 November 2026 and asked them to switch off auto-renew before each customer’s next renewal date. The End of AI Builder credits page gives the wider picture: on the same date, the AI Builder credits seeded into licences such as Power Apps and Power Automate premium also reach end of life. Existing add-ons and seeded credits stay usable until the contract term ends. The AI Builder features themselves aren’t going away; they run on Copilot Credits. An environment consumes AI Builder credits first, then Copilot Credits, and blocks the feature if neither is available. There’s no automatic conversion and no fixed ratio between the two; each scenario has its own rate. Why it matters. Every Power Automate flow that reads invoices or forms sits inside this change. My reading: the risky date isn’t 1 November but the day your current contract ends. If the environment has no Copilot Credits by then, flows start failing, and the first people to notice will probably be in accounts payable. I’d check two things this week: a list of flows that use AI Builder, and the licence renewal dates. On the budget side you’re moving from a fixed pack to consumption, which is hard to forecast if you don’t know your monthly document volume. They score a deployed agent against datasets of inputs and expected outputs, on demand or on a recurring schedule, and they run against the live agent rather than a design-time copy. The aim is to catch regressions, accuracy problems and unexpected behaviour without a manual test cycle. Production runs can be turned into test cases, so the dataset grows with the cases the agent actually sees. Why it matters. With classic RPA, a robot that worked yesterday works today. t: Agents get their own accounts, the EU’s first AI Act standard, a tax e-notice deadline
s: Issue three: agent accounts in Copilot Studio, the first harmonised standard under the EU AI Act, Türkiye’s new e-notification rules, UiPath audit-log and model changes, Maestro and a Gartner signal.
b: This week is about accounts and records. Microsoft is giving agents their own Microsoft 365 accounts, UiPath stopped logging prompts and responses by default in new AI policies, and Türkiye’s Revenue Administration rewrote the password and event-log rules for tax e-notifications. Brussels, meanwhile, delivered the first concrete compliance tool for high-risk AI. Copilot Studio: agent accounts, business process memory and triggers Microsoft Copilot Blog · 15 October 2026 Microsoft has started rolling out three Copilot Studio capabilities through its Frontier programme. With agent accounts, an agent works under its own credentials and scoped permissions instead of borrowing a user’s or maker’s identity; people can call it in Teams and Outlook and @mention it in Word, Excel and PowerPoint comments. Business process memory carries preferences and process context into the next cycle; makers switch it on, and users can view and delete what was saved. Triggers start an agent’s cycle from an external signal such as an e-mail, or on a set cadence, without a prompt. Admins can scope access and manage the agent’s lifecycle in the Power Platform admin center. Further access policies, cost management and lifecycle controls are planned “in the coming months”. The post gives no general-availability date, licensing or price. Why it matters. The robot-account question RPA teams have argued about for years has moved inside the office suite. An agent with its own identity is the right call for the audit trail, because it separates what the agent did from what a person did. My reading: an agent with a mailbox and a Teams presence sits squarely within the KVKK principle decision from last issue, and memory brings its own questions about retention and privacy notices. I wouldn’t multiply these accounts in production before the cost and lifecycle controls land. For a pilot, start simple: one owner, one purpose and a list of the channels each account may read. According to the Commission, providers of high-risk AI systems that apply it get a presumption of conformity with the Article 17 quality management requirements it covers. t: Türkiye limits workplace e-mail monitoring; agents get your own guardrails
s: Issue two: KVKK’s decision on monitoring work channels, UiPath agent review and bring-your-own guardrails, Orchestrator encryption, Google’s Gemini agent, the Boost.ai deal and a Gartner signal.
b: One question runs through this week: on whose behalf is a system acting, what is it looking at, and who allowed it? Türkiye’s data protection authority answered that for employee communications, while UiPath and Google shipped their own answers for agents. A short window, five days, but it includes an Official Gazette decision that reaches straight into automation design. KVKK: a principle decision on monitoring workplace e-mail and communication channels Official Gazette of Türkiye · 8 October 2026 (Board decision of 16 September 2026, No. 2026/2035) Türkiye’s Personal Data Protection Board published a 16-point principle decision on how employers may monitor corporate e-mail and other channels used for work. It isn’t limited to e-mail: internal messaging, CRM and ticketing systems, and chat and recording areas in meeting platforms are named too. Processing only traffic and log records, without opening content, still counts as processing personal data. A generic “your mailbox may be monitored” notice does not meet the duty to inform; the notice has to say concretely whether logs or content will be reviewed, when content may be accessed, and how long data is kept. Monitoring through tools that record everything an employee does, indiscriminately, is treated as unlawful. Access to the collected data should be limited to authorised staff and logged. Why it matters. It reads like an HR policy document, but automation teams are squarely in scope. A robot reading a shared mailbox, an agent watching Teams channels, or a task-mining tool recording every click on a desktop all operate in exactly these channels. My reading: “record everything and filter later” is no longer a defensible design. This week I’d check two things: the list of mailboxes and channels your robots and agents read, and who can see the logs and recordings those tools produce. If there’s no list, the privacy notice is probably incomplete as well. This isn’t legal advice; read the text with your legal team. Autopilot reviews an agent, lists critical issues, warnings and improvements, grades it from A to F by the number and severity of issues, and can apply the fixes in the same conversation. t: In an e-invoice robot, reconciliation is the real work
s: A robot that connects an ERP to Türkiye’s e-invoice infrastructure and reconciles the two. From 1 January 2027 small suppliers stop issuing paper invoices; what that changes in accounts payable.
b: When people hear “e-invoice robot” they usually picture “take the XML, write it to the ERP”. That is the easy half. The hard half is proving, every day, that two systems show the same truth: is every invoice on the e-invoice side also in the ERP, and does every ERP record rest on an actual document? This piece walks through a robot that connects an ERP to Türkiye’s national e-invoice infrastructure and produces a reconciliation report, and what 1 January 2027 means for flows like it. Why now General Communiqué No. 589 on the Tax Procedure Law, published in the Official Gazette on 31 December 2025, gave one more year to a specific group of taxpayers outside the e-Fatura and e-Arşiv systems: those on the simplified method or keeping business-account books. According to TÜRMOB’s circular, until 31 December 2026 they may still issue paper invoices up to 3,000 TL including taxes. From 1 January 2027 they must issue every invoice, whatever the amount, through the Revenue Administration’s e-Belge portal. For all other taxpayers the same rule has applied since 1 January 2026. Seen from the buyer’s side, the meaning is simple. For a company that buys from tradespeople and small suppliers, the paper channel into accounts payable largely closes in 2027. Almost every incoming invoice will be either e-Fatura or e-Arşiv. I noted this briefly in the first radar . The question here is more practical: is the robot you already run ready for it? What we delivered The e-invoice robot we built connects an ERP platform end to end with the national e-invoice infrastructure and produces a reconciliation report. We have built these integrations with Logo Tiger 3 and other ERP systems. I am not sharing the client’s name, volumes or internal detail. Some of the design notes below come from the backbone of that delivery and some from what I would add if I built a similar flow today; the labels in the walkthrough separate the two. The Revenue Administration states the basic rule plainly: two taxpayers registered in e-Fatura must send and receive the invoices they issue to each other as e-Fatura. An invoice to a buyer who is not registered is issued on paper or as e-Arşiv. So a company’s incoming invoice flow is not one format; it is fed by at least two. The robot’s first job is to tag that difference at the source. Why reconciliation is a separate job Integration says “record the incoming document”. t: Maestro splits in two, MCP goes stateless, and an e-invoice deadline lands
s: Issue one: the architectural split behind UiPath FUSION, Gartner’s warning on vendor-built agents, the new MCP spec, the EU AI Act calendar, Türkiye’s 1 January 2027 e-Arşiv rule and IXP’s new pricing unit.
b: As this is the first issue, the window is wider than a week. Six items from recent weeks that could change the budget, the architecture or the calendar of an automation programme. They share a thread: as the tools mature, the question moves from “can it do this?” to “who will own it, and what will it cost?” UiPath FUSION 2026: Maestro is now two products UiPath · 23 September 2026 At FUSION 2026 UiPath split Maestro in two. Maestro Orchestrate is for long-running processes that cross teams and systems; Maestro Automate is for small, fast, high-volume tasks. Several things went generally available in the same announcement: Cartographer, which drafts and maintains a “Map of Work” from documents, systems and people; UiPath for Coding Agents, which lets developers build with the coding agent they already use; and Delegate, a desktop agent. Dark Testing Factory is in preview and the Map of Work itself is on the roadmap. Why it matters. The split turns a decision teams already make into a product boundary. A case that stays open for weeks waiting on human approval and a queue item that finishes in seconds shouldn’t be governed by the same rules. Make that distinction in your architecture documents now: which processes hold state, and which only carry volume? I’d treat Cartographer as a way to keep the PDD current, not as a replacement for writing one. My first test would be a small process that already has documentation, comparing the output against what’s on file. Gartner: most vendor-built agents will be abandoned Gartner · 29 September 2026 Gartner’s 29 September release predicts that 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built by a vendor’s forward-deployed engineers by 2028. The published summary points to rising costs and to organisations being unable to evolve these systems on their own. Gartner’s page blocks automated access, so this item rests on the release title and its published summary. Why it matters. Outsourcing an agent build isn’t the problem. Being unable to maintain what you received is. I would put three things in the contract: versioned prompts and tool definitions, the evaluation sets used in acceptance testing, and at least one change made by the internal team alone after go-live. If the third can’t happen, what you have is a dependency, not a product. t: Catching anomalies in logistics: rules, a model and a person in one flow
s: The logistics anomaly detection we built with UiPath Maestro and agents: rule-based checks, classification with a language model and automatic notification to operations, plus the reasoning behind that division of labour.
b: Logistics data is a tempting place to ask a language model, “anything odd in these records?” The records are messy, description fields are free text, and the exceptions keep changing. Ask the model that question directly, though, and you lose two things: consistency and control over cost. The logistics anomaly flow we built with UiPath Maestro and agents splits the work three ways: rule-based RPA checks, classification with a language model, and automatic exception notification to operations stakeholders. This piece is about the reasoning behind that split. Don’t ask the model what a rule already knows If a mandatory field on a shipment record is empty, you don’t need a language model to say so. Same if a defined threshold is exceeded or the same record arrives twice. These checks are cheap, give the same answer every time, and are easy to explain in an audit. The model belongs where a rule can’t decide on its own. Free text is the clearest case, I think. The reason for a delay buried in an operations note, a phrase in a description field, what an inconsistency between two fields actually means: these are hard to capture with rules, and every new situation adds another rule. That’s where classification earns its place. The ordering has a side benefit. The model only sees records the rules flagged, so cost grows with the number of suspicious records rather than the total. Ask the model for a form, not an essay Binding the model’s output to a predefined schema is what keeps the rest of the flow solid. The anomaly type should come from a fixed list, the rationale should be short, and there should be a field where the model can say it isn’t sure. A model that returns free text forces every later step to guess. Writing the list of types with the operations team is part of the job. When something new shows up that isn’t on the list, a model that marks it as “other” is better than one that forces it into the wrong bucket. Notification is design work too Automatic notification can be the least discussed and most complained-about part of a flow. If everyone gets everything, soon nobody reads anything. When I design notifications I look at three things: Who receives it? The team or person responsible for that anomaly type. What do they see? The record, the anomaly type and a one-line rationale. Nobody should have to log in and search. When do they hear about it again? Not for the same anomaly, unless its status changes. Where Maestro fits Orchestration here means ru

t: Reading an invoice is not understanding it: on-prem document processing at an airline
s: The document-processing line we built for the finance team of a national flag carrier, running in the airline’s own data centre. Multi-language, multi-currency invoices, human validation and the decisions that shaped the design.
b: Reading the text on an invoice is no longer hard. OCR engines have done it well for years. The hard part is understanding what was read. Which amount is the total and which is a line? Which date is the invoice date and which is the due date? Is the table on page two a continuation of page one, or a separate breakdown? The document-processing programme we built for the Finance and Accounting function of a national flag carrier is built on that second question. It runs in the airline’s own data centre, processes supplier invoices end to end, and is live. Without going into the airline’s internal details, this piece walks through the decisions that shaped the design. The first constraint: documents don’t leave the building The first decision that shaped the architecture wasn’t technical. It was institutional: documents would not be sent outside the organisation. That’s a common requirement for finance documents and, I think, a fair one. A supplier invoice carries bank details, contract prices and payment terms. The consequence is that much of what you switch on with a few settings in the cloud becomes infrastructure work on-premises. Digitisation and extraction components have to run inside. Model versions, updates and capacity planning become part of the project. UiPath’s own documentation states that Document Understanding remains available for Automation Suite and Standalone deployments, which narrows the choice of product for any organisation with an on-premises requirement. The lesson here, as I see it, is simple: plan the on-premises installation as its own work item, not a deployment detail. If it isn’t in the schedule from day one, it will squeeze something later. Three gaps between reading and understanding The scope of this programme fits in three phrases: multi-currency, multi-language, multi-table. Each is its own problem. Multiple currencies. The currency isn’t always printed next to the amount. Decimal separators change from country to country, and the same supplier can change format over time. After extraction every amount has to be normalised and its currency checked against what the supplier usually invoices in. I’d leave that check to a rule, not the model. The model can be wrong; the fact that a supplier always bills in euros is already sitting in master data. Multiple languages. t: Document Understanding or IXP? A decision table by document type
s: A practical guide to choosing between UiPath’s two document-AI routes, starting from the document type, your generative-AI policy and where the system has to run. Grounded in UiPath’s own documentation.
b: UiPath now has two routes for documents, and the choice often starts in the wrong place: with “which one is newer?” A better starting point is the document itself. Two questions follow. How much generative AI does your organisation allow, and where will the system run? At BOTTEQ we build document-processing lines by combining Document Understanding with Base64.ai’s OCR/ICR engines. The table below doesn’t come from that work, though. It comes from UiPath’s own documentation, with the sources at the end. The commentary is mine. The two routes in brief Document Understanding (DU) is for structured and semi-structured documents: forms, purchase orders, applications, invoices. It works with pre-trained machine-learning models on documents whose layout is the same or very close. Its generative features can be governed through the organisation’s AI Trust Layer policies. DU continues as a standalone service and remains available on Automation Suite and Standalone deployments. IXP is the umbrella under which UiPath brought DU and Communications Mining together and added a new prompt-driven capability: generative extraction for unstructured and complex documents. UiPath describes it for annual reports, contracts and lease agreements. Complex tables, charts, checkboxes, signatures and handwriting, values that have to be inferred from context or stitched together across sections: that’s this route’s territory. Generative AI is mandatory here. Decision table Situation My recommendation Basis Forms, orders, applications, invoices with a largely fixed layout Document Understanding UiPath describes these as DU’s territory Contracts, leases, annual reports; values inferred from context IXP, generative extraction Complex structure, contextual inference and cross-section stitching are what this route is described for Emails, workflow tickets, short messages IXP, Communications Mining Built for short, free-text communication The organisation restricts generative AI Document Understanding Generative features can be governed here; they’re mandatory in IXP’s generative extraction Documents can’t leave the organisation Document Understanding DU continues on Automation Suite and Standalone; confirm IXP availability for your own deployment Long, multi-page files Check page limits first The documented limit for generative extraction is 50 pages, up to 150 in preview; up to 500 with DU activities Three questions the table can’t answer Mixed bundles. t: Seven questions before you give an agent decision rights
s: Most agentic projects stall over ownership, cost and risk control rather than technology. Seven questions I ask before go-live, with Türkiye’s KVKK guidance on agentic AI and the EU rules taken into account.
b: In June 2025 Gartner predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects would be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Model quality isn’t on that list. Agents mostly stall not because they can’t do the work, but because nobody is sure what they’re doing or what it costs. We’ve built change-management, monitoring and incident-response frameworks inside client organisations, and at the heart of that work is a plain fact: putting a system live means giving it authority. For RPA bots that authority was narrow; a bot followed steps someone had written down. An agent picks its own next step. So the questions you ask before signing off go-live change too. Here are mine. 1. Does it decide, or recommend? The same agent carries very different risk in the two roles. An agent that classifies a supply anomaly and puts it in front of a person is recommending. An agent that lifts a payment block on its own is deciding. Write this down for every action in the design document. “The agent does X” isn’t enough; say “the agent proposes X and this person approves” or “the agent does X and stops in this situation”. 2. Can a wrong decision be undone, and what does it cost? I suggest ranking actions on two axes: can it be reversed, and what does a mistake cost? Reversible, cheap actions can be left to the agent. Irreversible or expensive ones need a human approval gate. That gate isn’t an admission that the agent falls short; it’s a deliberate split of authority. Where the gate sits can change over time, too. As the records show the agent is reliable on a given type of action, you can pull the gate back. 3. Which tools can it reach, and under which identity? Every tool an agent can call is a list of everything it can do. An agent running with a human user’s permissions can make every mistake that user could. You need a separate service identity, only the tools it needs, and the narrowest permissions that work.
